claims.text: The median reported prevalence of cyberbullying among children and adolescents on social media is 23.0%.
Correlations between cyberbullying and anxiety among children and adolescents are inconsistent or weak.
Cyberbullying via social media is significantly associated with depression in children and adolescents.
Results regarding the association between cyberbullying and self-harm or suicidality are conflicting.
Relationship issues are the most common reason for cyberbullying.
Girls are most often the recipients of cyberbullying.
Responses to cyberbullying among children and adolescents are most often passive.

evidence.description: The median reported prevalence of cyberbullying was 23.0% (interquartile range, 11.0%-42.6%).
Five studies reported inconsistent and/or weak correlations between cyberbullying and anxiety.
Ten studies found a statistically significant association between cyberbullying and report of depression.
Five studies investigated self-harm or suicidality, with conflicting results.
Results indicate that the most common reason for cyberbullying is relationship issues.
Results indicate that girls are most often being the recipients of cyberbullying.
Responses to cyberbullying are most often passive, with a pervasive lack of awareness or confidence that anything can be done.

methodologies.name: Systematic review and narrative synthesis
methodologies.description: Systematic literature search across 11 electronic databases with dual reviewer screening, data extraction verification, and study quality assessment using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool.
conditions: Context of social media and cyberbullying
Target population of children and adolescents aged 12 to 18

limitations.text: Quantitative meta-analysis pooling of results was not possible due to heterogeneity in study objectives and outcomes.
